de25b_travel.topic: Who knows you travel: Secure Flight, Quiet Skies, APIS, PNR, ATS, CBP and TSA face capture, REAL ID, CLEAR, TSA-ICE sharing

claims.text: Secure Flight final rule (28 Oct 2008, effective 29 Dec 2008): TSA takes over watch-list matching from airlines; airlines must request full name, date of birth, gender, and redress or Known Traveler number if available; 'watch list' defined as the No Fly and Selectee components of the Terrorist Screening Database; TSA may use larger lists when security conditions warrant

Secure Flight PIA (9 Aug 2007): non-matches kept 7 days after travel; potential matches 7 years; confirmed matches 99 years; passport and itinerary data transmitted if available; program 'does not use algorithms to assign risk scores to individuals' and uses no commercial data

Quiet Skies ended 5 June 2025 by Secretary Noem, who called it 'a political rolodex of the Biden Administration'; it used an algorithm on travel patterns and other government data to send air marshals to watch travellers who were not on the FBI watchlist; cost about $200m a year (Washington Times); Gabbard said she was listed for criticising Harris; the reason for her listing remains unclear (CNN)

APIS pre-departure rule (23 Aug 2007, effective 19 Feb 2008): carriers transmit manifests (biographic page data) 30 minutes before doors close (batch) or up to door closing (interactive), for flights to and from the US; passengers who receive a 'not-cleared' response cannot be issued boarding passes

EU-US PNR Agreement (Council Decision 2012/472/EU): PNR includes name, travel dates and itinerary, ticket information, addresses and phone numbers, payment method and card number, travel agent, seat, baggage; kept up to 5 years in an active database (depersonalised after 6 months) then up to 10 years dormant; sensitive data deleted within 30 days. EDPS called a 15-year maximum 'clearly disproportionate' (Dec 2011, draft)

ATS PIA update (2017): ATS compares traveller data with law-enforcement and intelligence records using risk-based rules; ingests APIS, ESTA, visa, TECS, I-94, SEVIS and Secure Flight data for some flights; PNR is an ATS record; 'ATS is retaining ingested information consistent with its own 15-year retention period'; photo galleries of US citizens purged after processing, others kept 14 days

CBP biometric entry-exit final rule published 27 Oct 2025, effective 26 Dec 2025: CBP may photograph non-citizens on entry and exit at airports, land ports and seaports; US citizens are not covered and may take part voluntarily

TSA facial comparison at 84 airports (May 2025), plan for about 400; travellers may decline 'without recourse'; TSA says images deleted after verification, except PreCheck Touchless ID (24 h after departure) and testing

Algorithmic Justice League survey (via The Register, 31 Jul 2025): 74% said they were not warned facial recognition was used; Traveler Privacy Protection Act reintroduced May 2025 by a bipartisan group led by Sen. Merkley
REAL ID enforcement began 7 May 2025 under TSA final rule of 13 Jan 2025; the REAL ID Act 2005 followed a 9/11 Commission recommendation
From 1 Feb 2026 travellers without REAL ID or passport pay $45 for TSA ConfirmID, valid 10 days, using knowledge-based questions
CLEAR (Clear Secure, Inc.): founded 2003 as Verified Identity Pass; shut after bankruptcy 2009; bought 2010 by Caryn Seidman Becker and Ken Cornick; relaunched 2012; NYSE IPO 2021, ticker YOU

CLEAR FY2023 10-K: TSA selected CLEAR in Jan 2020 for PreCheck enrollment; operates under TSA Registered Traveler program; DHS SAFETY Act certification; links identity to 'eyes, face and fingerprints'; says it does 'never sell member data'
CLEAR FY2025 10-K: company says 'we are controlled by the Founder Post-IPO Members'; 'we do not sell our Members' data'
CLEAR FY2025 results (25 Feb 2026): 38.0m total members; 7.6m active CLEAR+ members; revenue $900.8m; 60 CLEAR+ airports; 340 retail locations with TSA PreCheck enrollment

CLEAR privacy notice (updated 26 Jun 2026): collects 'faceprints, fingerprints, iris scans'; shares data 'if required by law or legal process, including to governmental or regulatory bodies'; for CLEAR+ shares data 'with the Transportation Security Administration'; may share with third parties for advertising and marketing; 'does not sell your biometrics or sensitive Personal Data'; may retain data after account termination for fraud prevention

July 2022: CLEAR let through a passenger carrying ammunition who was travelling under a false identity; CLEAR called it 'a single human error'; TSA probed and required CLEAR members' IDs be checked by TSA officers (2023)
CLEAR contract with CMS (9 Dec 2025): CLEAR1 to be used for Medicare.gov account creation and recovery from early 2026; amount not disclosed

Reuters (7 Apr 2026): TSA gave ICE records on more than 31,000 travellers from Jan 2025 to Feb 2026; more than 800 arrests per internal ICE data; Secure Flight regulation says it was not intended to track immigration offenders

NYT first reported 12 Dec 2025 that TSA sends ICE passenger names multiple times a week, matched against final removal orders; partnership reportedly began March 2025; MOA signed May 2025; ICE stores TSA data in its own repository; MOA released in American Oversight v. TSA (D.D.C. 1:26-cv-00193); acting TSA administrator testified TSA does not 'send the information to ICE'

Secure Flight final rule: TSA calls the passenger data 'Secure Flight Passenger Data (SFPD)': full name, gender, date of birth and Redress Number, plus passport information if available and non-personal itinerary information and record locator numbers; aircraft operators send it through 'one DHS portal', approximately 72 hours before departure; TSA's boarding pass printing result lets the airline issue an unrestricted boarding pass, a boarding pass marked for enhanced screening (Selectee), or no boarding pass (inhibited) until resolved at the airport

ATS PIA update (DHS/CBP/PIA-006(e), 13 Jan 2017): ATS-P is 'a web-based enforcement and decision support tool'; UPAX is a technology refresh replacing the legacy ATS-P interface; 'ATS maintains the official record for Passenger Name Records (PNR)'; CBP ingests TSA Secure Flight Passenger Data in real time into ATS-P for overflights and US carrier point-to-point international flights; non-matching SFPD kept 7 days to create, modify and run rules

de25b_stop.topic: Who can stop you: passport law, no-fly litigation, debt passport denial, trusted-traveller revocation, exit-control comparators

claims.text: 8 U.S.C. 1185(b): unlawful 'for any citizen of the United States to depart from or enter' the country 'unless he bears a valid United States passport'; 1185(a) lets the President set rules for aliens' departure

Kent v. Dulles (16 Jun 1958): Secretary of State lacked authority to deny passports over alleged Communist beliefs and refusal to file affidavits; 'The right to travel is a part of the liberty' protected by the Fifth Amendment

Aptheker (1964): Section 6 of the Subversive Activities Control Act, denying passports to Communist Party members, unconstitutional on its face; 'too broadly and indiscriminately restricts the right to travel'
Haig v. Agee (1981, 7-2, Burger): upheld revocation (1979) of former CIA officer Philip Agee's passport for harm to national security; courts defer to executive
Terrorist Screening Dataset about 2m at end 2023 (1.16m in 2017; 120,000 in Dec 2003); vast majority not US citizens or LPRs; 'thousands of Americans'; no-fly count not given

Latif v. Holder (D. Or., June 2014, Judge Anna Brown): DHS TRIP 'wholly ineffective', violated due process; found 'a constitutionally protected, private interest in international travel by air'; government must give notice of status and reasons

Kashem v. Barr (9th Cir. 2019): No Fly criteria not vague as applied; revised (2015) procedures adequate under Mathews; TSA Administrator issues final orders, reviewable in courts of appeals under 49 U.S.C. 46110

FBI v. Fikre (19 Mar 2024, unanimous, Gorsuch): removal from the no-fly list with a pledge not to relist 'based on the currently available information' did not moot the suit; merits not decided; Fikre learned of listing in Sudan 2010, later detained and tortured in UAE

IRC 7345 passport denial: 'seriously delinquent tax debt' over $66,000 for 2026 (indexed; $51,000 in 2018, $64,000 in 2025); requires a filed lien with remedies exhausted or a levy; exclusions (installment agreement, CDP hearing, innocent spouse, bankruptcy, disaster area, hardship); CP508C notice; State may deny or revoke; 90 days to resolve; Tax Court or district court review; reversal within 30 days of resolution

Child-support passport denial (42 U.S.C. 652(k)): created by PRWORA 1996 at $5,000, lowered to $2,500 by the Deficit Reduction Act of 2005; states certify via OCSE to State's CLASS lookout system; nearly $621m collected since inception, $30m in 2024; existing passports revoked only when State holds them; H.R. 6903 would make revocation mandatory, passed House by voice vote 27 Apr 2026
H.R. 6903 received in the Senate and referred to the Finance Committee 28 Apr 2026; no further Senate action shown

22 U.S.C. 2714: no passport for a person convicted of a federal or state felony drug offense who used a passport or crossed a border in committing it, while imprisoned or on parole/supervised release; existing passports revoked; emergency or humanitarian exceptions

Sept 2025: House State Department authorization bill included a provision letting the Secretary deny or revoke passports of people he deems to have 'materially supported terrorists'; ACLU's Hamadanchy: 'a huge risk of abuse'; Chairman Mast filed a manager's amendment striking it (Intercept 15 Sep 2025; Guardian)

Feb 2020 DHS barred New York residents from trusted-traveller programmes over the Green Light Law; lifted 23 Jul 2020; government admitted in court that DHS statements were 'inaccurate and misleading'; NY AG James: 'political retribution, plain and simple'

Nicole Cleland (Minnesota): on 10 Jan 2026 a Border Patrol agent addressed her by name, said he had facial recognition; three days later her Global Entry/PreCheck was revoked; in a July 2026 suit (EPIC and three citizens, S.D. Cal.) claims under APA, Privacy Act, First Amendment; Ivey (revoked 10 days after observing in Charlotte Nov 2025, later reinstated) and Walker (restored after reporter's query); CBP denies retaliation; allegations untested
DHS (14 Feb 2026) said claims that Mobile Fortify violates the Fourth Amendment are 'false' and that it uses a 'deliberately high matching threshold'

Jackson-Vanik (Sec. 402, Trade Act of 1974): trade benefits conditioned on freedom to emigrate; bars a 'more than nominal tax on emigration'; Soviet 'education reimbursement fees' from Aug 1972, up to tens of thousands of dollars, affected mainly Soviet Jews emigrating to Israel or the US; stopped late 1972

Soviet citizens needed exit visas; refuseniks were 'denied exit visas for months, years, and even decades'; often fired, harassed; activists jailed; about 50,000 Jews left in peak year 1979; Gorbachev let most refuseniks leave from 1987

Safeguard Defenders 'Trapped' (2 May 2023): SPC database mentions of exit bans rose from under 5,000 (2016) to 39,000 (2020); with ethnicity-based bans total 'in the millions', others 'tens of thousands if not more'; at least 15 laws; Supervision Law allows bans on people connected to investigations; targets include rights defenders' families, foreign journalists, civil-dispute parties (O'Halloran nearly 3 years)

Russia law signed 14 Apr 2023: electronic summonses via Gosuslugi, deemed received 7 days after upload to the registry; recipients barred from leaving; after 20 days without reporting, barred from loans, property and vehicle registration, self-employment
July 2025: FSB border guards given direct access to draft data; a summons in the system bars a man from leaving; after 20 days, may be denied a foreign passport
